primary_sources: Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record, 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Representative Robert H. Clancy, speaking in the House of Representatives in 1924 against the immigration bill: Clancy said that newcomers had always faced bitter complaints, from the Irish and Germans of the 1840s to the Italians, Poles, Jews, Greeks, and Russians of his own day. He called the bill's use of the 1890 census “racial discrimination at its worst,” a deliberate attempt to aim a blow at the peoples of eastern and southern Europe.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record, 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924 (public domain, U.S. government). The quoted phrase “racial discrimination at its worst” is Clancy's own wording.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record, 1924, public domain

options.misconception: Immigration had not ended; the bill was written because newcomers were still arriving. Clancy's whole speech assumes they keep coming.

options.misconception: The Irish and Germans were the targets in the 1840s, not the welcomers. Clancy says they faced bitter complaints too.

options.text: Congress had always favored open borders
options.misconception: Congress was passing a quota bill in 1924. Clancy's point is that hostility kept returning, not that borders stayed open.

rationales.A: Immigration had not ended; the bill was written because newcomers were still arriving. Clancy's whole speech assumes they keep coming.
rationales.B: The Irish and Germans were the targets in the 1840s, not the welcomers. Clancy says they faced bitter complaints too.
rationales.C: Congress was passing a quota bill in 1924. Clancy's point is that hostility kept returning, not that borders stayed open.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Clancy lists group after group, decade after decade, facing the same complaints. His point is that each new wave meets the same hostility the last wave met.
rationales.general:
1. List the groups Clancy names: Irish and Germans, then Italians, Poles, Jews, Greeks, and Russians.
2. List the dates: the 1840s, then 1924.
3. Ask what stays the same across both lists: bitter complaints against the newest arrivals.
4. Name the move: he uses the past to show a pattern, not a one-time quarrel.
Remember: when a speaker lines up two eras side by side, ask what repeats and what changes.
